_about: Original texts written for LinguaSI demo data. The essays deliberately start with typical learner errors and improve over time so the demo learner's history shows realistic progress.
diagnostic_writing: I think living in a big city is more better than living in the countryside. Firstly, cities have more jobs and better universities, so young people can build a career. For example, my cousin moved to Dhaka and he find a good job in technology. However, cities are noisy and the air is polluted, and people has less time for their family. In conclusion, although the countryside is peaceful, but I prefer cities because they offer more opportunities.
diagnostic_speaking: My hometown is Sylhet, it is in the north east of Bangladesh. I like it because it is very green and there is many tea gardens. Um, the people is friendly and the food is delicious, so I really miss it when I am in Dhaka.

essays.text:
Nowadays, more and more people are choosing to work from home. In nowadays technology make this possible for many companies. In this essay I will discuss about the advantages and disadvantages of this trend.

Firstly, working from home has many advantages. People can save time and money because they do not need to travel to the office every days. For example, my brother spent two hours in traffic before, but now he can use this time for his family. Also, workers can organise theirselves and work in a quiet place, so they can not be disturbed by colleagues.

However, there is many disadvantages too. Some people feels lonely because they do not meet other people. It is also difficult to separate work and home life, and many workers work more longer than before. In addition, companies can not easily check if employees are working, and teamwork become harder.

In conclusion, although working from home save time, but it also cause some problems. I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages if companies give clear rules and workers take regular breaks.

Traffic congestion is a serious problem in many big cities around the world. This essay will explain the main causes of this problem and suggest some solutions.

The main cause of traffic congestion is the growing number of private cars. As people become richer, they prefer to drive their own car instead of using a bus or train. Another cause is poor public transport. In my city, Dhaka, buses are often crowded and unreliable, so people who can afford a car do not want to use them. Furthermore, many cities was not designed for so many vehicles, and the roads are too narrow.

There are several measures that could reduce this problem. Firstly, governments should invest on public transport, such as metro lines and modern buses. If public transport is fast and cheap, many drivers will leave their cars at home. Secondly, cities can introduce congestion charges in the city centre, as London did. This would encourage people to travel at different times or to share cars. Finally, companies could allow flexible working hours so that not everyone travels at the same time.

In conclusion, traffic congestion is mainly caused by the increase in private cars and poor public transport. However, with better investment and smart policies, it is possible to make our cities less crowded and more pleasant to live in.

Today, many young people spend several hours every day on social media platforms. In my opinion, this happens for a number of reasons, and although it has some benefits, it is mostly a negative development.

There are three main reasons why young people use social media so much. First, these platforms are designed to keep users scrolling, with endless videos and notifications. Second, social media is the main way teenagers communicate with their friends, so they feel they must be online to stay connected. Third, many young people use these apps to relax after school, because they are free and always available on their phones.

Some people argue that this trend is positive. Social media allows young people to share ideas, learn new skills from short tutorials and even start small businesses. For example, my cousin sells handmade jewellery through her online page.

However, I believe the disadvantages are more significant. Spending too much time online can affect on sleep and concentration, which may lead to lower grades at school. Moreover, constant comparison with others can damage young people's confidence and mental health. There is also a risk that teenagers spend less time on physical activity and face-to-face friendships, which are essential for their development.

In conclusion, young people use social media heavily because the platforms are addictive, social and convenient. While it offers some opportunities, I think the overall effect is negative, so parents and schools should teach young people how to use it in a balanced way.

The line graph compares the proportion of households with internet access in Avalia, Borenia and Cestria from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, internet access rose significantly in all three countries over the period. Avalia had the highest level throughout, while Cestria had the lowest, although it saw the most rapid growth after 2010.

In 2000, 42% of households in Avalia were connected to the internet, compared with 18% in Borenia and only 5% in Cestria. Over the next ten years, the figure for Avalia increased steadily to 78%, and Borenia's figure almost tripled to 52%. By contrast, access in Cestria grew slowly, reaching just 21% in 2010.

During the second decade, the gap between the countries narrowed. Avalia's figure continued to rise, but more gradually, finishing at 95% in 2020. Borenia climbed to 86%, while Cestria experienced the sharpest increase, more than tripling from 21% to 68%. Despite this, Cestria remained the least connected of the three countries at the end of the period.

Many governments face a difficult choice between investing in public transport and building new roads. I strongly agree that public transport should receive more funding, because it is more efficient, fairer and better for the environment.

Firstly, public transport moves far more people using less space. A single metro line can carry tens of thousands of passengers per hour, whereas a new road quickly fills with cars. Several cities have found that building more roads often creates more traffic, because driving becomes temporarily easier and more people choose it. Investing in trains and buses, on the other hand, reduces congestion in the long term.

Secondly, public transport is fairer to citizens. Not everyone can afford a car, especially students, elderly people and low-income families. Reliable and affordable buses give these groups access to jobs, education and healthcare. Money spent on roads mainly benefits drivers, who are often wealthier.

Finally, there are clear environmental benefits. Cars are one of the largest sources of air pollution and carbon emissions in cities. If more people travel by train or electric bus, the air becomes cleaner and countries can meet their climate targets more easily.

Admittedly, some roads are still necessary, particularly in rural areas where public transport is not practical, and for goods vehicles. However, these needs can be met by maintaining existing roads rather than building new ones.

In conclusion, I believe governments should prioritise public transport over new roads, as it carries more people, serves all members of society and helps to protect the environment.

Protecting the environment is one of the most urgent challenges of our time, and there is debate about whether individuals or governments should take the lead. While personal choices matter, I largely disagree that they are the best solution, because the scale of the problem requires strong government action.

It is true that individual behaviour can make a difference. When people recycle, reduce their meat consumption or choose public transport, they lower their own environmental footprint. Furthermore, these habits can spread through families and communities, gradually changing social norms. For instance, reusable shopping bags became popular partly because consumers chose them voluntarily.

However, individual efforts alone are unlikely to be sufficient. Most pollution and carbon emissions come from industry, energy production and transport systems, which ordinary citizens cannot control. A person may switch off the lights at home, but this has little impact if the national electricity grid still depends on coal. Only governments have the power to invest in renewable energy, set emission limits for factories and fund efficient public transport.

Moreover, laws create fair and consistent rules for everyone. Voluntary action tends to depend on awareness and income, as environmentally friendly products are often more expensive. Regulations such as bans on single-use plastics or taxes on fuel-inefficient vehicles change the behaviour of millions of people at once, and they also encourage companies to develop cleaner technologies.

In conclusion, although individuals should continue to make responsible choices, I believe government legislation is the most effective way to protect the environment. The ideal approach combines both, but laws must lead, because they address the main sources of damage and ensure that everyone contributes.

part1.text: My hometown is Sylhet, in the north-east of Bangladesh. What I like most is the green hills and the tea gardens, which are really peaceful in the morning. It has changed quite a lot since I was a child, because there are many more shopping malls and cafes now, but the countryside around it is still beautiful.

I'm a final-year student of computer science at a university in Dhaka. What I enjoy most is building small apps with my classmates, because we solve real problems together. The difficult part is the workload before exams. In the future I'd like to work as a software engineer, ideally for a company that builds tools for education.

In my free time I usually read novels or go for a walk in the park near my flat. I prefer spending time with a couple of close friends rather than in big groups. My hobbies have changed a bit, because as a child I played cricket every day, but now I'm more interested in photography.

I really enjoy Bengali food, especially fish curry with rice and a lot of spices. I usually prefer eating at home, because my mother is an excellent cook and it's healthier. I can cook a few simple dishes, like dal and vegetable curry, and I'm trying to learn more recipes this year.

The weather in Dhaka is usually hot and humid, and during the monsoon it rains heavily almost every day. My favourite season is winter, because it's cool and dry and perfect for spending time outdoors. To be honest, grey rainy days do affect my mood a little, so I try to stay busy.

I use my phone a lot, probably five or six hours a day, mostly for studying, messaging my family and watching tutorials. I couldn't live without my laptop, because all my university work is on it. Sometimes I think I spend too much time online, so I try to switch off notifications in the evening.

Yes, I enjoy reading a lot, especially detective novels and articles about science. When I was a child, my father bought me comic books every month, so I started reading early. I prefer printed books, because I like the feeling of paper, but e-books are more convenient when I'm travelling.

I like many kinds of music, but mostly I listen to Bengali folk songs and some pop music. I usually listen to music while I'm commuting or studying, because it helps me concentrate. I tried to learn the guitar when I was at school, but I gave up after a few months, which I regret now.

I don't play sports regularly now, but I go jogging twice a week. Cricket and football are by far the most popular sports in my country, and people get really excited during international matches. I prefer watching cricket with my friends rather than playing it, because it's more social.

Yes, I love travelling, especially to quiet places in nature, like hills or beaches. I usually prefer travelling with my family or a few friends, because sharing the experience makes it more memorable. In the future I'd really like to visit Japan, because I'm interested in its culture and technology.

I don't really enjoy shopping in crowded markets, so I usually buy things online, because it's faster and I can compare prices easily. The last thing I bought was a pair of headphones for my online classes. There's a small bookshop near my university that I visit regularly.

I don't have a lot of friends, but I have a few very close ones from school and university. We usually meet at a cafe on Friday evenings and talk for hours. I think a good friend is someone who is honest with you and supports you when things are difficult.

part2.text: I'd like to talk about a skill I would really like to learn, which is public speaking. I've wanted to improve it since my second year at university, when I had to give a presentation in front of about a hundred students and I was extremely nervous. My hands were shaking and I forgot half of what I had prepared. I think I would learn it by joining a debate club, because you get regular practice and honest feedback from other members. I would also watch recordings of good speakers and record myself practising at home. This skill would help me a lot in my future career, because software engineers often need to explain technical ideas to clients and managers who are not technical. It would also make me more confident in job interviews. So overall, I think public speaking is one of the most valuable skills I could develop in the next few years.

The place I'd like to describe is a small tea garden near my grandparents' village in Sylhet. I went there last winter during my semester break. It's on a gentle hill, and from the top you can see rows and rows of tea bushes stretching to the horizon. I spent most of the morning walking along the narrow paths, taking photos and talking to some of the tea workers, who were very friendly. I found it peaceful mainly because it was so quiet. In Dhaka there is constant traffic noise, but there I could only hear birds and the wind. The air was fresh and cool, and nobody was in a hurry. It made me realise how stressful city life can be, and I promised myself that I would go back at least once a year to relax and clear my mind.

I'd like to talk about my secondary school mathematics teacher, Mr Karim, who influenced me a great deal. I knew him for four years, because he taught our class from grade seven until our final exams. What made him special was the way he explained difficult problems with simple, everyday examples, and he never made anyone feel stupid for asking questions. He also ran a small computer club after school, which is where I wrote my first program. He influenced me in two important ways. First, he showed me that patience is essential when you're learning something hard. Second, he encouraged me to study computer science, even though my family originally wanted me to become a doctor. I still message him sometimes to tell him about my projects, and he always replies with useful advice.

The film I'd like to describe is a documentary about plastic pollution in the oceans, which I watched about a year ago with my university friends. It followed a team of scientists who travelled to different parts of the world and measured how much plastic was floating in the water and inside fish and sea birds. Some scenes were really shocking, especially the images of birds that had died because their stomachs were full of plastic. It made me think because I realised how much single-use plastic I personally used every day without noticing it. After watching it, I started carrying my own water bottle and shopping bag, and I convinced my family to reduce plastic packaging at home. I think it's a good example of how a film can actually change people's behaviour.

I'd like to talk about a time when I helped a younger student at my university who was struggling with programming. It was during my third year, and she had failed her first assignment and was thinking about changing her subject. I offered to meet her twice a week in the library, and we went through the basic concepts slowly, using small practical exercises instead of long theory. I also shared my old notes and showed her some free online courses. After about two months, she passed her next exam with a good grade, and she decided to continue with computer science. I felt really proud and happy afterwards, because I knew how difficult the first year can be. It also helped me understand the topics better, because teaching something is the best way to learn it properly.

The object I use every day is my laptop, which my parents gave me when I started university about three years ago. It's quite light and has a long battery life, so I take it everywhere. I use it for almost everything, from attending online lectures and writing assignments to coding projects and video calls with my relatives abroad. In the evening I sometimes use it to watch films or to practise English with online lessons. It's important to me not only because I need it for my studies, but also because it represents my parents' support, since it was quite expensive for our family. I take good care of it, and I always back up my files, because losing my work would be a disaster.

I'd like to describe a train journey from Dhaka to Chittagong that I took with my two best friends after our final school exams. We travelled by an overnight train, which was the first time any of us had travelled without our families. We booked a small cabin, brought a lot of snacks, and spent most of the night talking, playing cards and watching the villages pass by in the moonlight. In the morning we saw the sunrise over the paddy fields, which was absolutely beautiful. It was memorable because it felt like the beginning of our adult lives. We were a bit nervous about our results, but on that journey we felt completely free. Even now, whenever we meet, we still laugh about the funny things that happened on that train.

A goal I achieved was getting a scholarship for my university studies. I set this goal in my last year of school, because my family couldn't easily afford the tuition fees and I didn't want to put pressure on them. To achieve it, I created a strict study timetable, practised past exam papers every weekend and joined a study group with three classmates who had similar goals. I also had to write a personal statement, which I rewrote at least five times with help from my English teacher. When I received the email saying I had won the scholarship, I felt an incredible mixture of relief and pride. My parents were so happy that my mother cried. It taught me that long-term planning and consistency are more important than talent.

I'd like to talk about Pohela Boishakh, which is the Bengali New Year celebration in my country. It happens every year in the middle of April. On that day, people wake up early, wear traditional clothes, often red and white, and join colourful processions in the streets. In Dhaka there's a famous parade with huge masks and paintings made by art students. Families also eat traditional food such as panta bhat, which is rice soaked in water, with fried fish. It's important because it's a celebration for everyone, regardless of religion, so it brings the whole nation together. It also reminds young people of our culture and traditions, especially now that so much of our daily life is influenced by global trends and social media.

The app I'd like to describe is a language learning app that I've been using for my IELTS preparation. I found it about a year ago when a friend recommended it after she improved her band score. I mainly use it to practise vocabulary and writing, because it gives me short exercises every day and shows me the mistakes I make most often. What I find really useful is that it reminds me of words just before I'm likely to forget them, so I remember much more than before. It also tracks my progress, so I can see that my grammar accuracy has improved. It's useful to me because I'm busy with university, and it lets me study in short sessions on the bus or between classes, instead of needing hours at a desk.

part3.text: I think technology has changed things enormously. On the one hand, people can access information and courses instantly, which makes learning much more flexible. On the other hand, it can be distracting, and some people never develop deep concentration. In my view, the key is to teach young people how to use technology responsibly rather than simply limiting it.

In my opinion, schools should focus more on practical skills, such as managing money, communicating clearly and working in teams. These skills are essential in adult life, but many schools still concentrate mainly on memorising facts for exams. Of course, academic knowledge is important too, so ideally there should be a balance between the two.

I'd say people feel more stressed nowadays mainly because of work pressure and constant connectivity. Many people check their emails late at night, so they never really switch off. That's why green spaces in cities are so important, because they give people somewhere to relax, exercise and spend time with their families without spending money.

Travel has become much cheaper and easier in the last few decades, mainly because of low-cost airlines and online booking. This is positive because more people can experience other cultures. However, mass tourism can damage popular destinations, for example by raising house prices for local residents and harming the natural environment, so governments need to manage it carefully.

I think many people do measure success too much by money, partly because of advertising and social media, where people show off expensive possessions. Personally, I believe success also means having good relationships, good health and work that you find meaningful. Of course money matters, but beyond a certain level it doesn't make people much happier.

Traditional celebrations are important because they connect people to their history and give communities a shared identity. Globalisation is definitely changing them, for instance young people now celebrate international events like Valentine's Day, and some traditions are becoming more commercial. Still, I think festivals adapt rather than disappear, as long as families keep passing them on.

I think people still read a lot, but in a different way, because they read short articles and posts on their phones rather than long books. Films can definitely be a good way to learn about other cultures, as they show how people live, talk and solve problems. However, they sometimes present stereotypes, so it's better to combine them with other sources.

People volunteer for many reasons, for example to give something back to society, to meet new people or to gain experience for their careers. I think schools should encourage community service, but I'm not sure it should be compulsory, because volunteering is most valuable when people genuinely choose to do it.

speaking_answers.generic: I think it really depends on the situation. On the one hand, there are clear benefits, because people have more choices than in the past. On the other hand, there can be negative effects, especially for older people who find change difficult. For example, in my country many families are adapting to these changes, but it takes time, so I think the best approach is a balanced one.
